categories.description: Weaves, weights and choosing a cloth.

categories.name: Care
categories.description: Keeping a tailored suit for decades.

posts.title: Why we baste
posts.excerpt: A suit held together with white thread is a question, not an answer. Basting is how we ask it.
posts.content:
A basted jacket is a draft in cloth: long, loose stitches over a hand-padded canvas, made to be pulled apart.

At the first fitting we chalk the answers straight onto the cloth, unpick it and recut. It costs a week, and it is the week that makes the suit yours.

posts.title: Choosing a first cloth
posts.excerpt: Navy, a mid-weight worsted, and a weave you can wear four seasons out of five.
posts.content:
Most first suits should be navy: it is formal enough for a wedding and quiet enough for a Tuesday.

Choose around 280 g a metre. Heavier cloths drape beautifully but are hard work in June.

posts.title: Twenty-six measurements
posts.excerpt: What the tape records at a first measure, and the notes that matter more than the numbers.
posts.content:
We take twenty-six measurements, each twice. Then we stop measuring and watch how you stand.

A dropped shoulder, a forward neck, a wallet always on the left: these notes shape the pattern more than any single number.

posts.title: Reading chalk marks
posts.excerpt: Lines, crosses and arrows: the small language a cutter writes on cloth.
posts.content:
A straight line is a seam to move. A cross is a point that must not move. An arrow says take in, or let out.

The chalk brushes away, but the pattern keeps every mark for the next suit.

posts.title: Brushing, not cleaning
posts.excerpt: A clothes brush and a wooden hanger keep a wool suit for twenty years.
posts.content:
Brush down after every wear, against the nap then with it. Hang the jacket on a shaped wooden hanger for a day before wearing it again.

Dry cleaning flattens the canvas. Once a year is plenty; steam and rest do the rest.

posts.title: The last pressing
posts.excerpt: Why we press under a damp cloth, and how to keep the shape at home.
posts.content:
The final press sets the roll of the lapel and the line of the trouser crease. It takes longer than any other stage of finishing.

At home, a steamer and a cool iron through a cotton cloth are all you need.
